chapters.title: Chapter 1: Linear Algebra Basics for Machine Learning
chapters.description: Covers the core linear algebra concepts used throughout the paper: vector and matrix operations, inner products, orthogonality, matrix norms, eigenvalues, and singular value decomposition. Emphasis on interpretations relevant to neural networks (neurons as vectors, weight matrices as linear maps).
subtopics: Vectors and matrices: notation and basic operations (transpose, trace, rank)
Inner products and norms (L2 norm, Frobenius norm, operator/spectral norm)
Orthogonality and orthonormal bases
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; diagonalization
Singular value decomposition (SVD) and its interpretation
Relationships between SVD and spectral norm
Column/row spaces, nullspace, and implications for linear layers
Interpretation of neurons as column vectors of weight matrices

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Orthogonal Matrices and Their Properties
chapters.description: Introduces orthogonal matrices and the orthogonal group, their algebraic and geometric properties, parametrizations, and consequences for transform preservation. This chapter prepares the reader to understand orthogonality-preserving reparameterizations used in finetuning.
subtopics: Definition of orthogonal matrices and O(n) / SO(n) groups
Properties: inverse equals transpose, determinant ±1, preservation of inner products and norms
Geometric interpretation: rotations and reflections
Spectral properties and singular values of orthogonal matrices
Common parametrizations: Givens rotations, Householder reflections
Skew-symmetric matrices and the Lie algebra so(n)
Cayley transform: mapping skew-symmetric matrices to orthogonal matrices (and limitations)
Implications of left-multiplying a weight matrix by an orthogonal matrix

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Matrix Factorizations and Structured Matrices
chapters.description: Survey of structured matrix families and factorization techniques (low-rank, block-diagonal, sparse, permutations, Kronecker). Focus on how structure reduces parameter count and the expressivity/inductive-bias tradeoffs.
subtopics: Matrix factorization overview: motivations and use-cases
Low-rank decomposition (SVD truncation, rank-r factorization)
Block-diagonal and block-sparse matrices: definitions and effects
Permutation and diagonal matrices
Kronecker products and block structures
Trade-offs: parameter count vs expressivity vs computation
Structured sparse matrices and parameter-sharing
Examples of structured transforms in ML (e.g., circulant, Toeplitz)

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Fast Linear Transforms and the Cooley–Tukey Butterfly
chapters.description: Explains the Cooley–Tukey FFT algorithm and the butterfly computational structure. Presents the general idea of representing dense transforms as products of sparse factors and introduces classic fast transforms (DFT, DCT, Hadamard) that use butterfly-like patterns.
subtopics: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT): definition and properties
Cooley–Tukey radix-2 decomposition: recursive divide-and-conquer
Butterfly computational graph: stages, connections, and data flow
Butterfly factor as product of sparse matrices
Other fast transforms: DCT, DST, Hadamard transform and their butterfly-like structure
Permutation steps (bit-reversal) and stage-wise structure
Complexity analysis: O(n log n) vs O(n^2)
Practical considerations in implementing butterfly transforms

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Sparse Matrices, Storage and Efficient Multiplication
chapters.description: Covers sparsity representations, storage schemes, and algorithms for efficient sparse matrix-vector and sparse-sparse multiplication; discusses how sparsity patterns affect computation and parameter efficiency.
subtopics: Sparsity definitions and common patterns (banded, block-sparse, random sparsity)
Compressed storage formats: CSR, CSC, COO
Complexity of sparse matrix-vector and sparse matrix-matrix multiplication
Permutation and block permutations for exposing sparsity
Impact of sparsity pattern on memory access and compute efficiency
Sparsity and trainable parameters: counting effective degrees of freedom
Trade-offs: computation (time) vs storage (space)
Numerical issues arising from extreme sparsity

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Numerical Linear Algebra and Stability
chapters.description: Addresses numerical stability, conditioning, and stability of algorithms that manipulate orthogonal and structured matrices. Discusses how spectral properties affect optimization and generalization in deep networks.
subtopics: Matrix conditioning and condition number
Stability of orthogonal transforms and their numerical benefits
Rounding error and accumulation in staged matrix products
Preservation of spectral norm under orthogonal transforms
Effects of ill-conditioning on gradient-based optimization
Techniques to improve numerical stability (rescaling, reorthogonalization)
Practical numeric considerations when composing many sparse factors

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Optimization Methods in Deep Learning
chapters.description: Introduces core optimization algorithms and best practices used in finetuning large models: SGD, momentum, Adam variants, learning rate scheduling, initialization, regularization, and dropout. Includes multiplicative vs additive parameter updates and their consequences.
subtopics: Gradient descent, SGD with momentum, and adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSprop)
Learning rate selection and scheduling strategies
Initialization methods and zero/identity initializations
Regularization techniques: weight decay, early stopping, dropout
Dropout: additive vs multiplicative viewpoints and variants
Additive parameter updates (e.g., LoRA) vs multiplicative updates (layer-wise transforms)
Batch normalization and layer normalization effects during finetuning
Practical tips for stable finetuning of large pre-trained models

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Parameter-Efficient Finetuning (PEFT) Techniques
chapters.description: Survey of methods for adapting large pretrained models with limited trainable parameters. Discusses motivations, representative algorithms, and the different structural choices (low-rank, adapters, prompt tuning, orthogonal transforms).
subtopics: Problem statement: why parameter-efficient finetuning is needed
Fine-tuning vs full retraining: costs and trade-offs
Adapter modules: addition of small subnetworks
Prompt tuning and prefix tuning for transformer models
Low-rank adaptation (LoRA): formulation and practice
BitFit and other minimal-parameter approaches
Orthogonality-based finetuning approaches (concepts without specific novel methods)
Metrics for comparing PEFT methods (parameter count, performance, latency)

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Graph Theory and Communication/Information Transmission Models
chapters.description: Presents graph-theoretic concepts and communication network models used to reason about staged information exchange. Supplies a vocabulary for describing layered grids, paths, connectivity, and broadcasting relevant to factorized matrix constructions.
subtopics: Basic graph concepts: nodes, edges, paths, connectivity
Layered or grid graphs and directed acyclic topologies
Broadcast and multicast trees, butterfly networks as communication topologies
Connectivity requirements for complete transmission between layers
Counting edges and degrees of freedom under constraints
Graph-theoretic interpretations of matrix multiplication (unrolled computation graph)
Implications of graph sparsity on information flow and expressivity
Network design metrics: latency, bandwidth, and redundancy parallels

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Optimization on Matrix Manifolds
chapters.description: Covers the theory and practice of optimizing matrices under constraints (e.g., orthogonality). Introduces manifold optimization concepts, retractions, and constrained parameterizations used to maintain orthogonality during optimization.
subtopics: Manifolds and tangent spaces: intuition and simple examples
Orthogonal group as a Riemannian manifold
Retractions and exponential map versus practical retractions
Constrained optimization methods: projected gradient, manifold-aware optimizers
Parametrizing orthogonality: Cayley transform, exponential map, Givens rotations
Computational trade-offs of various parametrizations
Practical implementation issues: invertibility, numerical stability, and cost

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Signal Processing Perspective and Inductive Biases of Transforms
chapters.description: Links classical signal-processing transforms to inductive biases in learning. Explains why particular structured transforms (Fourier, DCT, Hadamard) are useful and how their architectures inject priors that can aid generalization.
subtopics: Frequency-domain intuition and basis transforms
Sparsity in transform domains and energy compaction (e.g., DCT for images)
Localized vs global transforms and their inductive biases
How structured linear operators encode priors for natural data
Examples: convolution as structured linear map, circulant matrices
Use of fast transforms in feature extraction and kernel approximation
Relation between transform structure and model generalization

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Bilinear Forms, Metric Learning and Similarity Models
chapters.description: Introduces bilinear similarity forms and metric learning, connecting orthogonal transforms to distance-preserving and similarity-based modeling used in representation learning.
subtopics: Bilinear forms and quadratic forms: definitions and properties
Mahalanobis distance and linear metric learning
Bilinear similarity models in classification and retrieval
Interpretation of left-multiplying weights as learning a bilinear map
Regularization via orthogonality in metric learning
Connections between orthogonal transforms and invariant similarity measures

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Complexity Analysis and Time–Space Trade-offs
chapters.description: Analyzes computational complexity and parameter-count trade-offs when choosing structured parameterizations. Discusses how trading computation (more staged multiplications) for fewer parameters affects training/inference cost and storage.
subtopics: Counting trainable parameters for various structures (dense, low-rank, block-diagonal, butterfly-like)
Time complexity of forward and backward passes for staged products
Space complexity and memory footprint during training
Latency considerations at inference vs training
Asymptotic analyses (O(d^2), O(d log d), O(d)) and constants
Practical profiling: FLOPs, memory bandwidth, and cache effects
Design considerations for parameter-budget allocation across layers

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Practical Architectures and Finetuning Pipelines
chapters.description: Describes modern neural architectures (transformers, vision models, diffusion models) and the practical steps and engineering concerns involved when finetuning large pretrained models in real workloads.
subtopics: Transformer architecture: attention, feed-forward layers, layer normalization
Vision transformer and convolutional backbones: linear layers characteristics
Text-to-image diffusion models: basic pipeline and where linear transforms appear
Where to apply parameter-efficient modules in large models (which layers, shared vs per-layer)
Checkpointing, mixed precision, and memory-saving techniques
Batching, data pipelines, and dataset considerations for finetuning
Evaluation protocols: validation splits, overfitting checks, and metrics

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Experimental Design and Measuring Expressivity
chapters.description: Guides how to empirically evaluate structured parameterizations: how to design approximation experiments, measure expressivity and approximation error, and perform ablations that isolate sources of improvement.
subtopics: Designing matrix approximation experiments (random orthogonal targets, error metrics)
Measuring approximation error: Frobenius norm, spectral norm, angle-based metrics
Ablation studies: controlling parameter counts, block sizes, and stages
Statistical considerations: repeatability, random seeds, confidence intervals
Visualization of sparsity patterns and information flow
Benchmarks and baselines for PEFT comparisons
Interpreting results: expressivity vs generalization trade-offs
